summary: Return the squares of a non-decreasing array sorted in non-decreasing order.
mainInsight: The largest square is at one of the ends. Use two pointers at both ends and fill the result from the back, taking the larger square each time and moving that pointer inward. This is O(n) instead of squaring and sorting in O(n log n).

approaches.name: Square then sort
approaches.summary: sorted(x * x for x in nums).

approaches.name: Two pointers from both ends
approaches.summary: Fill the result from the end with the larger square.

commonMistakes: Using absolute values in the wrong order
Forgetting that all-negative or all-positive arrays are valid

cards.answer: Two pointers at both ends, filling the result from the back with the larger square. Clue: The input is sorted but contains negatives, so the largest square is at one of the two ends; compare the ends and fill the output from the largest down.
keyPoints: The input is sorted but contains negatives, so the largest square is at one of the two ends; compare the ends and fill the output from the largest down.
cards.explanation: Squares are largest at the extremes of a sorted array, so each step takes the bigger of the two end squares.

rubric.technique: Two pointers at both ends, filling the result from the back with the larger square

alsoValid.name: Square every element and sort

rubric.clue: The input is sorted but contains negatives, so the largest square is at one of the two ends; compare the ends and fill the output from the largest down.

promptVariants: Why does the largest square always lie at one of the two ends?
options: Large negatives square to large values, so a maximum sits at an end
The largest square is always the last element of the array
The largest square always sits somewhere in the array's middle
The largest square always belongs to the value nearest zero
cards.answer: Large negatives square to large values, so a maximum sits at an end
cards.explanation: The array is sorted by value, not by absolute value.

incorrectOptionExplanations.The largest square is always the last el: A large negative at the front can be larger in magnitude.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The largest square always sits somewhere: Near zero the squares are smallest.

promptVariants: Why fill the result from the back?
What would happen if you filled it from the front?
cards.answer: The pointers at the ends give the largest remaining square, so each step determines the next largest value. Filling from the front would need the smallest square, which lies in the middle near zero and requires a different pointer strategy.
cards.explanation: Alternative: start at the sign change and merge outward.

cards.explanation: Compare |-6| = 6 and 7; 49 is placed at the end, then 36 vs 25, and so on.

incorrectOptionExplanations.[1, 4, 25, 36, 49] after comparing 36 an: The result is right, but the comparison starts at both ends: 6 vs 7.
incorrectOptionExplanations.[4, 1, 25, 36, 49]: the sign change is n: 1 is smaller than 4, so 1 must come first.
